s: Conduct is expressive if there is an intent to convey a particularized message and a great likelihood it will be understood (Spence v. Washington; Texas v. Johnson, 1989, flag burning).
Students do not "shed their constitutional rights… at the schoolhouse gate."
Schools may restrict speech that would materially and substantially disrupt (Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969).
Further allowances cover lewd speech (Fraser), school-sponsored expression (Hazelwood), and promotion of illegal drugs (Morse v. Frederick).
Off-campus speech receives more protection (Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., 2021).

Buckley v. Valeo (1976) distinguished contributions, where limits are permissible to prevent quid pro quo corruption or its appearance, from expenditures, where limits get strict scrutiny and generally fail.
Citizens United v. FEC (2010) struck limits on independent expenditures by corporations and unions.
McCutcheon (2014) struck aggregate contribution limits, and FEC v. Cruz (2022) struck a limit on repaying candidate loans.
Disclosure requirements receive "exacting scrutiny" (Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta, 2021, requiring narrow tailoring).

The government may not compel affirmation of beliefs (West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943, the flag salute; Wooley v. Maynard, 1977), require speakers to host messages (Hurley, 1995), or compel the creation of expressive products contrary to the speaker's message (303 Creative LLC v. Elenis, 2023).
Compelled factual disclosures in commercial advertising get relaxed review (Zauderer), but not in other settings (NIFLA v. Becerra, 2018).
Expressive associations may exclude members when inclusion would significantly burden their message (Boy Scouts v. Dale, 2000).
